project_name: BioValue AI demo: fictional softwood kraft lignin stream
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.

constraints: The lignin is currently used as internal boiler fuel, so diversion to an external product route would need to account for the displaced fuel use.
The stream leaves the mill as wet filter cake and no lignin dryer is available, limiting buyers or pathways that require dry powder unless drying is added externally or on site.
Solvent or membrane fractionation and chemical-modification equipment are not available, limiting value-added pathways that require those processing steps.
Covered cake storage is available, but wet-cake handling and shipping remain practical constraints for external markets.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are missing, so pathway and buyer-specification screening cannot be completed for requirements involving those properties.
The data are fictional assumptions rather than mill measurements, so operating, quality, and commercial decisions cannot rely on this profile without replacement data.
data_quality_notes: The record is explicitly fictional demo data; the mill, stream, and all values are invented assumptions rather than measurements from a real mill.
The annual wet quantity and moisture conversion results are validated, and the recorded dry-matter balance passes.
The recorded composition check passes, but lignin-content analytical method clarity is flagged as a data gap.
Moisture is uncertain and should be logged over time because it affects dry tonnage and shipped mass.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are not measured and must be supplied before relevant pathway comparisons.
The profile includes assumed annual ranges and illustrative analytical methods; these should be replaced or confirmed with mill records and laboratory methods.
agent.summary: Validated fictional profile for a washed softwood kraft lignin filter cake: 40000.0 t/yr wet mass, 0.35000000000000003 moisture fraction, and 26000.0 t/yr dry mass. The data are not decision-ready because the record is fictional and key chemical properties are missing.

lignin_pct.method: Acid-insoluble (Klason) plus acid-soluble lignin, as % of dry matter (method stated for illustration)

sulfur_pct.method: Total sulfur by elemental analysis (stated for illustration)

carbohydrates_pct.method: Total sugars after acid hydrolysis (stated for illustration)

checks.detail: recorded dry matter 26,000 t/yr; wet quantity x (1 - moisture) = 26,000 t/yr
lignin + ash + carbohydrates = 96.5% of dry matter
3 missing figure(s), each with a data-gap entry

data_gaps.impact: Every figure in this profile is invented for demonstration. Results based on it say nothing about a real mill.
data_gaps.next_step: Replace the profile with the mill's own lab data and production records.

data_gaps.impact: Molecular weight can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of molecular weight distribution, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: Phenolic hydroxyl content can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of hydroxyl group content, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: The make-up of the ash is unknown, so ash-related requirements can only be checked against total ash.
data_gaps.next_step: Request an inorganic element analysis of the ash.

data_gaps.impact: Reported lignin content depends on what the analysis counts. The method here is stated for illustration only.
data_gaps.next_step: Confirm the analytical method with the lab and use the same one when comparing with buyers' specifications.

data_gaps.impact: Moisture sets the dry tonnage (dry matter = wet quantity x (1 - moisture)) and the mass that has to be shipped.
data_gaps.next_step: Log cake moisture for each shift over at least one month.

checks.disclaimer: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.

current_use.description: Fictional: the precipitated lignin is fired in the mill's own boilers in place of purchased fuel. The unit was built to relieve the recovery boiler, not to sell lignin.

geographic_market.logistics: Fictional: rail siding at the mill; the nearest deep-water port is assumed to be about 150 km away.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#1: UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#2: Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#3: UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#3: A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.
supported_claims.EV-PF-03#1: A techno-economic comparison lists LignoBoost extraction combined with phenol substitution in resins ('LB+Resin') at TRL 9.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can be used as a partial phenol replacement in phenol-formaldehyde resins for plywood and other wood-based-panel adhesives.
Lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin is reported for veneer plywood and can meet Bonding Class 3 under EN 314-2.
The evidence reports phenol replacement up to 50% for kraft lignin using a two-step process, while a vendor reports replacement up to 80% for its lignin product.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers include plywood manufacturers and producers of wood-based panels that use phenol-formaldehyde adhesives.

competing_materials.statement: The principal incumbent material is phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resin formulations.

qualification_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin requires an activation or depolymerization step before use in phenol-formaldehyde resins.
Reported plywood qualification includes EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 and formaldehyde-emission testing under EN 717-2.
One laboratory study evaluated resin viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde against a Chinese wood-adhesive standard, but the paper names that standard inconsistently.

limitations: The replacement levels are drawn from studies or vendor literature rather than a single commercial-plant demonstration.
The EN 314-2 and EN 717-2 performance claims are vendor-reported without a cited test report.
The reported depolymerized-lignin molecular-weight range is not established as a specification for mill-delivered lignin.
The laboratory evidence used poplar plywood samples, and the cited Chinese standard is identified inconsistently.
missing_information: No lignin purchase price, sales volume, named buyer, contract term, or regional demand is provided.
No evidence establishes whether the fictional wet filter-cake stream can meet a buyer's moisture, ash, molecular-weight, or phenolic-hydroxyl specifications.
The evidence does not quantify drying, activation, or depolymerization costs for this stream.
The evidence does not identify a commercial customer for the fictional stream.

market_evidence.rationale: The pathway has documented industrial-proven and high-readiness claims, including a vendor-reported plywood application and a reported TRL 9 resin route, but the library does not document commercial sales to established buyers. This supports documented development or industrial evidence rather than the higher scores reserved for commercial sales.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#1: Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#2: Unmodified lignin reduced foam resiliency: compression set rose to 7-32% against 6% for the control, though it stayed within the standard's limit of below 60%.
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

applications.statement: Lignin can partially replace petroleum-based polyol in rigid polyurethane or polyisocyanurate insulation foam.
Lignin can partially replace petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam; kraft lignins produced denser and stiffer foams that may suit heavy-duty foams.
The evidence also covers lignin-based polyurethane panels, coatings, and rubber-replacement uses, although the pathway evidence rates polyurethane uses collectively at TRL 6.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers include rigid insulation-foam producers and other polyurethane foam manufacturers.

Automotive flexible-foam producers are a potential customer type, although the evidence found organosolv lignins more suitable for automotive flexible foam and suggested kraft lignins for heavy-duty foam.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is petroleum-based polyol used in polyurethane formulations.

qualification_requirements.statement: One study assessed rigid PUR/PIR foam against ASTM C1029-15 Type 1 specifications.

A cited acceptable range for rigid polyurethane production is total hydroxyl value above 200 mg KOH/g, equivalent in that source to 3.56 mmol/g total hydroxyl; this is not a phenolic-hydroxyl specification.
Kraft lignin generally needs significant treatment, such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction, to reach target polyurethane properties.
Flexible-foam testing compared performance with automotive OEM requirements, including a compression-set limit below 60%.

limitations: Most evidence is from laboratory foam studies rather than commercial production.
The rigid-foam study covered multiple lignin types and did not establish a kraft-lignin-only pass rate in its headline result.
The flexible-foam study did not measure sulfur odor despite identifying it as a known drawback of some softwood kraft lignins.
The market and readiness evidence covers polyurethane uses collectively, not a specific commercial product or kraft-lignin grade.
A recent review was available only as an abstract, limiting detail on its commercialization assessment.
missing_information: No lignin price, polyurethane-grade sales volume, named buyer, contract term, or regional demand is provided.
No evidence establishes whether this stream's missing total hydroxyl value, molecular weight, sodium content, moisture, ash, viscosity, or odor profile meets a polyurethane buyer's specification.
The evidence does not provide the cost or equipment requirement for drying, oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction for this stream.
The evidence does not identify commercial sales of kraft-lignin polyurethane products to established buyers.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence shows research-scale foam trials and a development/readiness assessment, but it does not document commercial sales, named buyers, or a commercial polyurethane-lignin product. This fits interest demonstrated primarily in research literature and announcements.

supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#1: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#2: The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#R1: Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#3: Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.

applications.statement: Softwood lignin can serve as a precursor for carbon fiber, but the evidence identifies purification and a plasticizing agent as necessary for the examined kraft or softwood lignin route.

Kraft lignin can be converted into hard carbon for sodium-ion battery anodes; the review reports higher initial coulombic efficiency for hard carbon made from kraft lignin than from sulfonated lignin in the compared study.
Lignin can be converted into activated carbon, including when its quality is too low for other carbon-material uses.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers include carbon-fiber precursor and carbon-fiber producers.
Potential customers include sodium-ion battery-material manufacturers and battery manufacturers or carmakers involved in anode-material qualification.
Activated-carbon producers are a potential customer type because the evidence directly evaluates lignin as an activated-carbon precursor.

competing_materials.statement: PAN-based carbon fiber is an incumbent competing precursor or material for carbon fiber.
Anthracite is a fossil-derived competing feedstock identified for sodium-ion battery hard carbon.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited ORNL carbon-fiber precursor specification requires lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, volatile material below 5% at 250 °C, and removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
Residual carbohydrates for the cited carbon-fiber precursor specification must be below 500 ppm.
Softwood lignin requires a plasticizing or alloying agent for melt spinning, and the examined kraft lignin required purification before carbon-fiber use.
Activated carbon has no strict precursor-quality limitation in the cited study, although higher ash reduced activated-carbon yield and carbon conversion.
Battery-material qualification can take 3 years according to the cited company material.

limitations: The carbon-fiber specifications are cited secondhand and are the most demanding carbon-material requirements; they do not apply automatically to hard carbon or activated carbon.
The carbon-fiber studies include non-kraft or generalized softwood lignin evidence, and the DOE findings date from the FY2009 progress report.
The GreenLight cost and readiness results are a project summary with modelled costs, not independently verified measured commercial performance.
The hard-carbon evidence is a review of sodium-ion battery studies, while the company qualification evidence concerns lithium-ion batteries and provides no lignin quality specifications.
The activated-carbon evidence is laboratory-scale and used zinc chloride activation.
missing_information: No lignin price, carbon-material sales volume, named buyer, contract term, or regional demand is provided for the fictional stream.
No evidence establishes whether the stream meets the carbon-fiber requirements for lignin purity, ash, volatiles, residual carbohydrates, or particulates.

The feedstock profile does not provide the molecular-weight, sodium, or other quality data needed to screen some carbon-material routes, and the evidence does not supply a buyer-specific specification for hard carbon or activated carbon.
The evidence does not quantify the drying, purification, spinning, carbonization, activation, or battery-qualification cost for this stream.
The evidence does not establish commercial sales of products made from this fictional lignin stream.

market_evidence.rationale: The pathway has documented development activity, including precursor-fiber validation in an industrially relevant environment, a pilot production line announcement, and battery-manufacturer or carmaker qualification activity. However, the library does not document several producers selling to established buyers, so it does not support scores 4 or 5.

processing_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin requires an activation or depolymerization step before use in phenol-formaldehyde resins.
The resin would require customer qualification, including plywood bonding and formaldehyde-emission testing reported against EN 314-2 and EN 717-2.

technical_maturity.statement: The LignoBoost extraction combined with phenol substitution in resins is reported at TRL 9, although that maturity claim does not qualify this fictional wet stream.

adoption_barriers.statement: Commercial adoption requires activation or depolymerization before resin use, while the mill profile states that chemical-modification equipment is unavailable.

The reported replacement levels and plywood performance come from studies or vendor literature rather than a single commercial-plant demonstration, and the cited performance claims lack a cited test report.
Potential customers are plywood and wood-based-panel manufacturers, but no commercial customer for the fictional stream is identified.

assumptions: The economics tool used fictional wet-feedstock assumptions of 36000.0, 40000.0, and 43000.0 t/yr in the conservative, base, and optimistic scenarios.
The economics tool used fictional moisture assumptions of 40.0%, 35.0%, and 30.0% of wet mass in the conservative, base, and optimistic scenarios.
The economics tool assumed that 40.0%, 50.0%, and 60.0% of dry lignin would be available for the pathway in the conservative, base, and optimistic scenarios.
The economics tool calculated dry mass of 21600.0, 26000.0, and 30100.0 t/yr and usable dry feedstock of 8640.0, 13000.0, and 18060.0 t/yr across those scenarios.

The economics tool did not assume product yield, product price, or variable costs; therefore product output, revenue, variable cost, gross contribution, and contribution per tonne were not calculated.
No value was assigned to the lignin's current internal boiler-fuel use.
The profile is treated as a fictional screening case rather than decision-ready mill data.
uncertainties: Feedstock compatibility received no deterministic score because the evidence library supplied no numeric phenolic-resin requirements to check against the profile.
Indicative economics cannot be judged because product yield, product price, and variable costs are missing; profitability, NPV, and IRR also remain uncalculated.
Wet-cake handling, drying requirements, displaced boiler-fuel value, and the missing chemical-quality data could materially change feasibility.
The cited studies do not establish whether this fictional wet filter-cake stream meets a buyer's specifications.

commercialization_feasibility.rationale: This is a technically mature route with identifiable panel-adhesive customers, but the mill would need drying and chemical-modification capability and a qualification partner before commercial adoption. That matches the rubric level for a route needing major new assets and partners that are not yet identified.

feedstock_compatibility.rationale: The evidence library has no numeric requirements for this pathway to check against.

technical_readiness.rationale: TRL 9 maps to 5. Stated in EV-PF-03#1.

indicative_economics.rationale: Gross contribution per tonne was not calculated. Not calculated: needs gross contribution, which could not be calculated. Missing inputs: product yield, product price, variable costs.

processing_requirements.statement: For carbon fiber, the kraft-lignin route requires purification, and softwood lignin requires a plasticizing or alloying agent before melt spinning.

The cited carbon-fiber precursor specification requires lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, volatile material below 5% at 250 °C, residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, and removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
For activated carbon, activation is required; the cited route has no strict precursor-quality limitation, although lower ash improves yield and carbon conversion.

technical_maturity.statement: Lignin precursor-fiber production in the GreenLight project reached TRL 5, validated in an industrially relevant environment; this applies to precursor-fiber production rather than the complete lignin-to-carbon-fiber chain.

adoption_barriers.statement: The carbon-fiber screening found lignin content of 94 versus a requirement greater than 99 and ash of 1 versus a requirement below 0.1, producing a compatibility score of 1 for the checked requirements.

The profile does not provide the quality data needed to screen carbon-fiber requirements for volatiles, residual carbohydrates and particulates, while the route also requires purification and melt-spinning preparation.

Activated carbon offers a less restrictive precursor screen, but the cited evidence is laboratory-scale and uses zinc chloride activation; hard-carbon and battery routes still require buyer-specific qualification.

main_drivers: Only pathway ranked because it has 0.8 assessed weight, above the 0.6 completeness threshold; attractiveness is 2.19 with a range of 1.95–2.75.
Technical readiness and market evidence both score 3, supported by TRL 5 precursor-fiber validation, pilot activity, and qualification activity.

Feedstock compatibility scores 1 because the checked carbon-fiber requirements show a large relative gap; commercialization feasibility scores 2 because major conversion assets, process development, and qualification partners are unresolved.
Indicative economics was not assessed, so the ranking is provisional. Evidence quality is high overall, with 3 high-quality and 2 moderate-quality cited records.
what_could_change_it: A measured activated-carbon or hard-carbon trial that meets a buyer's specification could improve the pathway's compatibility assessment and strengthen its rank.
Failure to meet lower-specification carbon-material requirements, or unfavorable drying, purification, activation, and qualification costs, could move it down.
Measured product yield, product price, variable costs, and the value of displaced boiler fuel could materially change its attractiveness once economics is assessed.

The assessed criteria are favorable: technical readiness scores 5, market evidence scores 3, and commercialization feasibility scores 2.
Feedstock compatibility and indicative economics remain unassessed. Drying, chemical modification, buyer specifications, product yield, product price, and variable costs are unresolved.

Attractiveness is 3.45 with a range of 2.35–4.15, showing substantial upside if compatibility and economics are demonstrated. Evidence quality is high overall, with 2 high-quality and 1 moderate-quality cited records.
what_could_change_it: Measured phenolic-hydroxyl, molecular-weight, moisture, ash, and sodium data that meet a resin buyer's specification could make feedstock compatibility assessable and improve its position.

A successful trial using the actual wet cake, including drying and resin performance testing, could support commercialization feasibility; inability to meet panel-adhesive specifications could move it down.
A sourced resin yield, product price, variable-cost case, and buyer commitment could move it above carbon materials after it becomes rankable.

main_drivers: Not ranked because only 0.55 of the weighted criteria were assessed, below the 0.6 completeness threshold.
Technical readiness scores 3, market evidence scores 2, and commercialization feasibility scores 2; the evidence is mainly research-scale or development-stage rather than commercial.
Feedstock compatibility and indicative economics remain unassessed. Total hydroxyl value, molecular weight, sodium, moisture, ash, viscosity, odor, yield, price, and variable costs are unresolved.
Attractiveness is 2.36 with a range of 1.75–3.55. Evidence quality is high overall, with 2 high-quality and 1 moderate-quality cited records.
what_could_change_it: Measured hydroxyl, molecular-weight, sodium, moisture, ash, viscosity, and odor data that meet a polyurethane buyer's specification could make compatibility assessable.

A successful oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction trial with acceptable foam performance and treatment yield could improve technical and commercialization confidence; poor performance or high treatment costs could move it down.
A named buyer, product price, yield, and variable-cost case could make the route rankable and improve its position; lack of a qualification partner could weaken it.

validation_steps.action: Replace the fictional feedstock profile with representative wet filter-cake measurements, including molecular weight, phenolic-hydroxyl content, sodium, moisture, ash, and pathway-specific quality properties.
validation_steps.reason: The stream is fictional and key properties are missing, preventing compatibility screening for phenolic resins and polyurethanes and limiting interpretation of carbon-material routes.

validation_steps.action: Run bench or pilot conversion trials for each pathway using the actual wet cake, including drying and any required chemical modification, and measure product yield and performance.
validation_steps.reason: This tests whether the stream can be converted at the claimed readiness levels rather than relying on generalized or non-stream-specific evidence.

validation_steps.action: Obtain written specifications and qualification requirements from at least one potential buyer for each route, including acceptable moisture, ash, molecular-weight or hydroxyl ranges, and product performance criteria.
validation_steps.reason: No established buyer, contract term, regional demand, or buyer-specific specification is documented for the fictional stream.

validation_steps.action: Build a route-level contribution model using measured yield, product price, variable costs, drying and conversion costs, capital costs, and the displaced boiler-fuel value and replacement-fuel cost.
validation_steps.reason: Indicative economics was not assessed for any pathway, and external diversion must account for the lignin's current internal fuel use.

validation_steps.action: Assess partner and asset options for drying, purification, chemical modification, carbonization, activation, and downstream qualification, with budgetary quotes and an implementation schedule.
validation_steps.reason: All pathways require capabilities not currently available at the mill, while the carbon-material route additionally depends on major conversion and qualification infrastructure.

ranking_changers: A measured phenolic-resin compatibility result plus a credible resin yield, price, and variable-cost case could make phenolic resins rankable and potentially move it above carbon materials; its current attractiveness range is 2.35–4.15.

A measured carbon-material route result showing that the actual stream can meet a lower-specification activated-carbon or hard-carbon target could improve carbon-material compatibility; failure in those routes would weaken the current rank-1 position.

A commercial polyurethane buyer specification and successful treatment trial, combined with positive yield and contribution economics, could move polyurethanes from insufficient data into the ranking and materially improve its position.
Product yield, product price, and variable costs for all three pathways are the largest common missing inputs; completing them could change both attractiveness and ranking.
The value of displaced boiler fuel and the cost of replacement fuel could materially change the economics of every external pathway.
caveats: The feedstock profile is explicitly fictional and must be replaced with mill measurements before operating or commercial decisions.

The ranking is deterministic and provisional: carbon materials is ranked first because it is the only pathway above the 0.6 completeness threshold, not because it has the highest fully evidenced business case.
Phenolic resins and polyurethanes are listed as insufficient data, not as poor pathways; each has 0.55 assessed weight.
Indicative economics was not calculated for any pathway because product yield, product price, and variable costs are missing; profitability, NPV, and IRR were not calculated.
The carbon-material compatibility score is driven by checked carbon-fiber requirements; activated carbon and hard carbon may have different requirements and should be assessed separately.
No pathway has a demonstrated commercial sale, named buyer, contract term, or regional demand for this fictional stream.
report.summary: The deterministic engine ranks carbon_materials first at 2.19, but only provisionally because economics is missing and feedstock compatibility is weak for the checked carbon-fiber requirements. Phenolic_resins has the strongest upside, with attractiveness 3.45 and a range of 2.35–4.15, but is insufficient data because compatibility and economics are unassessed. Polyurethanes is also insufficient data, with attractiveness 2.36 and a range of 1.75–3.55. The immediate priority is measured feedstock characterization, pathway trials, buyer qualification, and a complete contribution model that includes displaced boiler-fuel value.
